summary:
Orbital Trade-off is a browser game in which players plan a complete space mission. They choose the science questions to answer, build the spacecraft from 57 parts, pick one of 15 real rockets and an orbit, launch, fly to one of nine destinations, and read a report on the results.

Every part adds mass, uses power, produces data and costs money, and live meters show the effect at once. A rocket with too little Δv never arrives. After each mission the game flies it again with one choice changed at a time, so players see what each decision was worth and which change would help most. In Team Mission, up to four players share one device. Each owns one part of the design with its own goal, and the team must agree at a GO/NO-GO review before launch.

Students usually learn orbits, rockets and spacecraft as separate topics, but real missions depend on how those choices fit together. Our game lets them practise that, fail safely and try again. It runs offline on a laptop, iPad or phone, with nothing to install.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Orbital Trade-off is a game where you plan and fly a space mission from start to finish. A mission starts with the science: players choose which questions to answer, and each question needs its own instrument. Next they build the spacecraft and rocket from 57 parts. Each part has mass, power draw, cost, data output and heat. Live meters show the mass margin, power, budget, data, link budget and Δv as parts go on. The rocket is one of 15 real launchers. The game uses the rocket equation to check whether it can reach the chosen orbit or planet.

Players then launch in 3D, fly to one of nine destinations from Earth orbit to Titan, and run the spacecraft in mission control. The whole mission is simulated: solar power drops with distance from the Sun, the data rate drops with distance from Earth, memory fills up and parts can fail. At the end, a report scores the mission and explains the result.

There are several ways to play:

- Mission Sprint: nine five-minute missions with star ratings, for beginners.

- Campaign: the full NASA project life cycle, from a proposal against rival teams through design reviews (PDR, CDR), ground tests and launch day to operations and disposal.

- Team Mission: one to four players share one device. Each takes a role with its own goal: Principal Investigator (science), Spacecraft Engineer (power and reliability), Comms & Operations (data), Mission Manager (rocket and budget). Players take turns on their own decisions. Then everyone votes GO or NO-GO at a design review, and a NO-GO sends the design back to the role that has to change. After launch the team handles one in-flight emergency together. Teams are scored out of 1000 and ranked on a leaderboard.

- Workshop and Sandbox for free building, plus three difficulty levels and random events.

BENEFITS

- Players learn by trying. A failed mission costs nothing, and a new design can be flown in about a minute.

- The game explains each result. After every mission it flies the same mission again with one choice changed at a time, and shows what each decision was worth and which single change would help most. The Trade-off Lab does the same while you build.

- It runs on the devices schools already have. It is one HTML file that works offline in any modern browser on a laptop, iPad or phone, with no install or account.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want teachers, science clubs and students to use it to learn mission design as one connected problem rather than as separate topics. The team mode lets them practise the kind of negotiation real mission teams go through, where science, engineering, operations and budget pull in different directions.

TOOLS

- HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks. A small Node.js script packs everything into one file.

- WebGL for the 3D launch sites, ascent and landings. Canvas 2D for the menus, maps and charts. Web Audio for sound effects and music generated in the browser.

- Data: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble Earth imagery, JPL planet positions for launch windows, and NASA/JPL-based maps of the other planets.

- Playwright for automated tests: full playthroughs, a physics test, and layout checks on 13 screen sizes.

- We used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant, while writing and testing the code.

- No special hardware: we developed on ordinary laptops and tested in desktop and mobile browsers.

WHAT IS CREATIVE ABOUT IT

- Results show the value of each choice in numbers, so trade-offs can be measured rather than guessed.

- In team mode the roles' goals conflict on purpose, so the team has to negotiate before it can launch.

- Every team flying the same mission meets the same in-flight emergency, so scores can be compared fairly. How the emergency plays out depends on what the team chose earlier. For example, buying spare reaction wheels turns a wheel failure into a non-event.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Realism against simplicity. The game uses real relationships (the rocket equation, solar power falling with the square of distance, data rate falling with the square of distance) but simplifies elsewhere. The climb to orbit uses a 1:20 scale Earth, and the real values are shown beside the game ones.

- Beginners. A five-minute first mission comes with a guide, the language is plain, and every science question names the instrument that answers it.

- Fairness and balance. We simulated 324 designs per mission to set the team goals and star ratings. On every mission at least one design meets all four goals, but the obvious design does not.

- Access. It works offline, starts quickly on slow phones and fits screens from a 320-pixel phone to a laptop.
